Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Minh is a 69-year-old widowed man of Vietnamese descent who spent most of his working life as a nanny, caring for other people’s children. The trauma that reshaped his world occurred four years ago, when he was watching three-year-old Leo, a boy he had looked after since infancy. One afternoon, Leo became suddenly unresponsive, his skin hot and mottled. Minh called 911, but the minutes before the paramedics arrived stretched into an eternity he could never later reconstruct. The boy was diagnosed with a severe bacterial infection that led to septic shock. Leo survived after weeks in the pediatric intensive care unit, but Minh never recovered.

Now, when he tries to explain what happened, the story comes out in fragments. He cannot tell it clearly, even to himself. The memory does not unfold like an ordinary recollection. Instead, it arrives as a full sensory assault — the smell of Leo’s sweat, the odd angle of his small arm, the sound of his own voice on the phone with the dispatcher — and it feels more real than anything around him. Minh will be washing dishes, and suddenly he is back in that living room, the boy limp in his arms, the sirens still blocks away. The memory has no past tense. It is happening now, and he cannot stop it.

To cope, Minh learned to snap his mind away from these intrusions. He keeps himself occupied from the moment he wakes until he collapses into bed. He watches television shows he does not follow, folds laundry that is already neat, replays old songs in his head. He avoids any thought that might lead back to that afternoon. But the effort exhausts him, and the memories still break through. He also avoids medical care entirely. He has not seen a doctor in over three years, even for routine checkups. The sight of a clinic waiting room, the smell of antiseptic, the sound of a child crying — any of it can trigger a flashback so vivid that he feels he might pass out.

The consequences have been severe. Minh stopped working as a nanny shortly after the incident. He could not bear to be around any child who might become ill; every cough or fever felt like the beginning of another collapse. His employer understood, but without his income, he struggled to maintain his small apartment. He became withdrawn. He had always trusted people easily — it was part of why he was good with children — but now he finds himself scanning faces for hidden dangers. People are not what they seem, he believes. They carry illness, or they hide their true intentions. Even his own daughter, who calls every week, feels distant to him. He cannot explain to her what happened because he cannot explain it to himself.

What frightens Minh most is the person he has become. He used to be warm, patient, quick to laugh. Now he is rigid and watchful. He feels permanently damaged, as if the event carved something essential out of him and left a stranger in its place. That stranger does not recognize his own reflection. He finally agreed to seek help because his daughter pleaded with him, and because he is terrified of spending the rest of his life in this state. He does not know if therapy can undo what was done. But he is desperate enough to try, even if it means walking into a clinic where the air smells faintly of disinfectant and a child’s cough echoes down the hall.
